sections.name: The 12 Principles of Animation
sections.explanation_simple: The 12 principles of animation were created by Disney animators in the 1930s and they're STILL the foundation of ALL animation today - from Pixar movies to Fortnite dances to Nintendo games. These principles aren't optional rules - they're what separates professional animation that feels alive from amateur animation that feels robotic. Think of them as the grammar of movement: you need to know the rules before you can break them effectively.
key_concepts: 1. Squash and Stretch: Objects squish when hitting something and stretch when moving fast (gives a sense of weight and flexibility)
2. Anticipation: A small movement backward before a big movement forward (wind-up before a punch, crouch before a jump)
3. Staging: Presenting an action clearly so the audience sees it (positioning, timing, camera angle)
4. Straight Ahead vs Pose-to-Pose: Drawing frame-by-frame vs setting key poses and letting computer interpolate
5. Follow Through and Overlapping: Parts keep moving after the main action stops (hair settling, coat flapping)
6. Slow In and Slow Out: Objects accelerate and decelerate smoothly, not at constant speed (ease-in, ease-out)
7. Arcs: Most natural movement follows curved paths, not straight lines
8. Secondary Action: Smaller actions that support the main action (facial expressions while walking)
9. Timing: Number of frames determines the speed and weight of an action
10. Exaggeration: Pushing poses and expressions beyond realistic for clarity and impact
11. Solid Drawing: Making 3D characters feel solid and three-dimensional with proper weight
12. Appeal: Characters should be interesting and engaging to watch (charm, design, personality)

code_examples.title: Animation Curves: Graph Editor Mastery
code_examples.code:
# ===== GRAPH EDITOR CURVE TYPES =====
"""
Blender's Graph Editor: The most important tool for animation.

KEY CURVE TYPES:

1. CONSTANT (Step) - No interpolation, instant change
   Uses: Blinking, toggle switches, sudden events
   
2. LINEAR - Constant speed from A to B
   Uses: Mechanical movement, robots, conveyor belts
   
3. BEZIER - Smooth acceleration/deceleration (default)
   Uses: Most natural movement
   
4. SINE WAVE - Smooth oscillation
   Uses: Breathing, idle bobbing, pendulums

IMPORTANT HANDLE TYPES:
  - Auto: Blender smooths automatically
  - Vector: Sharp corner (linear on both sides)
  - Aligned: Handles are always a straight line (smooth)
  - Free: Each handle moves independently

GRAPH EDITOR SHORTCUTS:
  V - Change handle type
  S - Scale selected keyframes
  Alt+S - Scale the curve values
  T - Interpolation mode menu
  Shift+E - Extrapolation mode (cyclic, linear, constant)
"""

# Python: Set animation interpolation
import bpy

def set_keyframe_interpolation(action_name, interpolation="BEZIER"):
    """Change interpolation type for all keyframes in an action."""
    if action_name not in bpy.data.actions:
        print(f"Action '{action_name}' not found")
        return

    action = bpy.data.actions[action_name]
    for fcurve in action.fcurves:
        for keyframe in fcurve.keyframe_points:
            keyframe.interpolation = interpolation

    print(f"Set all keyframes in '{action_name}' to {interpolation}")

# Usage:
# set_keyframe_interpolation("WalkAction", "BEZIER")

# ===== CYCLIC ANIMATION (Walk cycles, breathing loops) =====
def make_cyclic(action_name):
    """Make an animation loop seamlessly."""
    if action_name not in bpy.data.actions:
        return

    action = bpy.data.actions[action_name]
    for fcurve in action.fcurves:
        # Set extrapolation to cyclic
        fcurve.extrapolation = 'CYCLIC'

    print(f"Made '{action_name}' cyclic")

# make_cyclic("RunCycle")

sections.name: Body Mechanics & Character Performance
sections.explanation_simple: Body mechanics is about making characters move with realistic weight, balance, and physics. When a character walks, their hips rotate, their shoulders counter-swing, their head bobs, and their weight shifts from foot to foot. Getting body mechanics right is what separates professional game animation from amateur. Good body mechanics make characters feel heavy, alive, and grounded. Bad body mechanics make characters feel like floating mannequins.
key_concepts: Weight Shift: Transferring weight from one foot to the other (essential for all locomotion)
Center of Gravity: The balance point of the character (hips area for humans)
Contact Poses: The moment a foot hits the ground (the most important pose in a walk cycle)
Passing Pose: The moment both feet pass each other (legs straight, hips leveled)
Up/Down Motion: The natural bob as a character walks (lowest at double support, highest at passing)
Twist: The rotation of hips and shoulders in opposite directions (counter-animation)
Foot Roll: Heel down -> flat -> toe push-off (essential for natural walks)
Arm Swing: Arms counter-swing to legs (right leg forward, left arm forward)
Follow-Through: Body parts that keep moving after the main action stops
Overlap: Different body parts start/stop at different times (hair, clothing, fat jiggle)
Drag: A part that lags behind (a heavy sword being dragged)
Lead: A part that initiates movement (head leads the body, elbow leads the arm)
sections.learning_path: Pelvis and hip movement -> Walk cycle (contact, down, passing, up, contact) -> Run cycle -> Weight lifting -> Pushing/pulling -> Jumping and landing -> Fighting poses -> Emotional body language -> Quadruped walks

sections.name: VFX: Fire, Smoke, Explosions & Magic
sections.explanation_simple: Visual effects (VFX) are the fire, smoke, explosions, magic spells, and environmental effects that make games and films exciting. In games, VFX run in real-time on the GPU using particle systems (thousands of tiny sprites or meshes that move with physics rules). In films, VFX are simulated offline with physics solvers (Houdini is the industry standard). The trick to great VFX is layering: a single explosion might have 5+ layers (core flash, expanding fire ring, smoke cloud, debris particles, shockwave ripple). Each layer uses different physics, colors, and timing.
key_concepts: Particle Systems: Thousands of small sprites that simulate fire, smoke, sparks
GPU Particles: Particles simulated on the graphics card (millions possible)
CPU Particles: Particles simulated on the processor (thousands only, but more control)
Spawn Rate: How many particles are created per second
Lifetime: How long each particle lives before disappearing
Initial Velocity: Speed and direction when particle is born
Drag/Air Resistance: Slows particles down over time
Turbulence/Noise: Random movement for organic-looking effects
Color Over Life: Particle changes color as it ages (yellow -> orange -> black for fire)
Size Over Life: Particle grows or shrinks (explosion expands)
Texture Sheet Animation: Flipbook animation on particles (like a mini-movie per particle)
Additive Blending: Bright particles glow (fire, lightning, magic)
Alpha Blending: Semi-transparent particles (smoke, fog)
EmberGen: Real-time fire/smoke simulation tool (game changer for VFX)
Niagara (UE5): Unreal's next-gen VFX system
VFX Graph (Unity): Unity's GPU particle system
Fluid Simulation: Actual physics simulation of liquids and gases (expensive, for films)

code_examples.title: Creating a Fireball in UE5 Niagara
code_examples.code:
# ===== UNREAL NIAGARA FIREBALL VFX =====
"""
SYSTEM: Fireball_Projectile
This creates a fireball that flies through the air leaving a trail.

EMITTER 1: Fireball Core (Single particle)
  - Render: Sphere mesh
  - Material: Emissive orange with noise distortion
  - Emitter Update:
    - Set Lifespan = lifetime of projectile
    - Spawn Burst: 1 particle
  - Particle Update:
    - Location updates every frame via Blueprint
    - Scale: Uniform 50 units
    - Color: Orange (1,0.4,0) with pulsing intensity

EMITTER 2: Smoke Trail (Continuous)
  - Render: Sprite with smoke texture (additive)
  - Emitter Update:
    - Spawn Per Second: 50 particles
  - Particle Spawn:
    - Position: Offset from core (-10 in Z)
    - Velocity: Random direction (100 units/s)
    - Lifetime: 0.5-1.0 seconds
    - Size: 10-30 units
  - Particle Update:
    - Scale Color Over Life: Orange -> Dark Gray -> Transparent
    - Scale Size Over Life: 1.0 -> 3.0
    - Drag: 0.5 (slows down over time)
    - Add Velocity Noise: Random wobble

EMITTER 3: Spark Trails
  - Render: Sprite with star texture
  - Emitter Update:
    - Spawn Per Second: 20 particles
  - Particle Spawn:
    - Position: Random around core (radius 5)
    - Velocity: Outward burst (50-200 units/s)
    - Lifetime: 0.3 seconds
    - Color: Bright yellow (1,0.8,0)
  - Particle Update:
    - Scale Color Over Life: Yellow -> Transparent
    - Drag: 0.9 (stops quickly)

EMITTER 4: Glow (for impact)
  - Triggered by "On Impact" event
  - Single burst of 200 particles expanding outward
  - Bright white to orange fade
"""

// Niagara spawning from C++
UNiagaraComponent* SpawnFireball(UWorld* World, UNiagaraSystem* FireballEffect, FVector Location, FRotator Rotation)
{
    UNiagaraComponent* NiagaraComp = UNiagaraFunctionLibrary::SpawnSystemAtLocation(
        World,
        FireballEffect,
        Location,
        Rotation
    );

    if (NiagaraComp)
    {
        // Bind to update location every frame
        // Use a timeline or tick to update User.ProjectilePosition
        NiagaraComp->SetNiagaraVariableVec3(FName("ProjectilePosition"), Location);
    }

    return NiagaraComp;
}

sections.name: Physics Simulation: Cloth, Hair, Fluids & Destruction
sections.explanation_simple: Physics simulation makes things move automatically based on real-world physics rules. Cloth simulation makes capes flow and flags wave. Hair simulation makes characters' hair and fur move naturally. Fluid simulation makes water, lava, and goo flow and splash. Destruction simulation makes buildings crumble realistically. Each type of simulation uses different math: cloth uses spring networks, fluids use particle or grid-based solvers, and destruction uses rigid body physics with constraint breaking. In real-time games, these are simplified for performance. In films, they're full physics simulations that can take hours to compute per frame.
key_concepts: Cloth Simulation: Mesh vertices connected by springs (stretch, shear, bend springs)
Pinning: Parts of cloth that stay in place (shoulders of a cape, collar of a shirt)
Wind Force: Natural airflow affecting cloth, hair, foliage
Self-Collision: Cloth doesn't pass through itself (important for skirts, loose clothing)
Hair/Fur: Each strand is a chain of particles with stiffness and gravity
Guide Hairs: Base hairs that determine the shape, then interpolate thousands of render hairs
Fluid Simulation (SPH): Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics - water as particles
Fluid Simulation (Grid): Water as a 3D grid of pressure/velocity values (more accurate, slower)
Flip Fluids: Hybrid particle + grid method (industry standard for film-quality water)
Rigid Body Simulation: Solid objects with physics (mass, friction, bounciness)
Constraints: Connections that break under force (glue holding bricks together)
Active vs Passive: Active objects are physics-controlled, passive are static colliders
Destruction: Breaking objects into pieces that then simulate as rigid bodies
Caching: Saving simulation results to disk so you don't need to re-simulate

code_examples.title: Blender Cloth & Hair Simulation Setup
code_examples.code:
# ===== BLENDER CLOTH SIMULATION =====
import bpy

def setup_cape_simulation(cape_mesh_name="Cape", character_mesh_name="Character"):
    """Set up cloth simulation for a character's cape."""

    cape = bpy.data.objects.get(cape_mesh_name)
    character = bpy.data.objects.get(character_mesh_name)

    if not cape or not character:
        print("Meshes not found")
        return

    # Select the cape
    bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = cape
    cape.select_set(True)

    # Add cloth modifier
    cloth_mod = cape.modifiers.new(name="Cloth", type='CLOTH')

    # Configure cloth settings
    cloth_mod.settings.quality = 10  # Higher = better but slower
    cloth_mod.settings.time_scale = 1.0
    cloth_mod.settings.mass = 0.3  # Light fabric
    cloth_mod.settings.tension_stiffness = 15.0  # How stretchy
    cloth_mod.settings.compression_stiffness = 15.0
    cloth_mod.settings.shear_stiffness = 10.0
    cloth_mod.settings.bending_stiffness = 0.5  # How much it flops
    cloth_mod.settings.air_damping = 1.0
    cloth_mod.settings.internal_friction = 0.0
    cloth_mod.settings.collision_quality = 5

    # Pin the shoulders (vertices at the top of the cape)
    # In edit mode, select vertices that should stay on the shoulders
    # Then click "Pin" in the cloth settings

    # Add wind force
    bpy.ops.object.effector_add(type='WIND', location=(5, 0, 3))
    wind = bpy.context.active_object
    wind.field.strength = 10.0
    wind.field.noise = 2.0  # Gusty wind

    # Set character as collision object
    character.select_set(True)
    bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = character
    cloth_collision = character.modifiers.new(name="ClothCollision", type='COLLISION')
    cloth_collision.settings.damping_factor = 0.1
    cloth_collision.settings.friction_factor = 0.5

    print(f"Cape simulation set up on {cape_mesh_name}")
    print("Press Alt+A to play the simulation")

# setup_cape_simulation("Cape", "Character_Mesh")

# ===== BLENDER HAIR SYSTEM =====
def setup_hair_system(head_mesh_name="Head"):
    """Set up hair particles on a character head."""

    head = bpy.data.objects.get(head_mesh_name)
    if not head:
        print(f"Mesh '{head_mesh_name}' not found")
        return

    bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = head
    head.select_set(True)

    # Add hair particle system
    hair_mod = head.modifiers.new(name="Hair", type='PARTICLE_SYSTEM')
    psys = hair_mod.particle_system
    psys.settings.type = 'HAIR'

    # Configure hair
    settings = psys.settings
    settings.count = 10000  # Number of hair strands
    settings.hair_length = 0.3  # 30cm hair
    settings.hair_step = 5  # Segments per strand

    # Children (interpolated hairs between guide hairs)
    settings.child_type = 'INTERPOLATED'
    settings.child_nbr = 50  # 50 children per guide hair
    settings.rendered_child_count = 100

    # Physics
    settings.mass = 0.1
    settings.mass_shape = 0.5  # Thickness
    settings.bending_stiffness = 0.5  # How rigid
    settings.bending_damping = 0.1
    settings.tension_stiffness = 0.0
    settings.random = 0.1  # Random variation

    # Render as paths (for Cycles)
    settings.render_type = 'PATH'

    # Material
    hair_mat = bpy.data.materials.new(name="Hair_Material")
    hair_mat.use_nodes = True
    # Set up Principled Hair BSDF node
    nodes = hair_mat.node_tree.nodes
    nodes.clear()
    principled = nodes.new('ShaderNodeBsdfHairPrincipled')
    principled.inputs['Color'].default_value = (0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 1)  # Dark brown
    principled.inputs['Melanin'].default_value = 0.8  # How dark

    output = nodes.new('ShaderNodeOutputMaterial')
    hair_mat.node_tree.links.new(principled.outputs['BSDF'], output.inputs['Surface'])

    head.data.materials.append(hair_mat)

    print(f"Hair system set up with {settings.count} guide hairs")

# setup_hair_system("Character_Head")

sections.name: Motion Capture & Retargeting
sections.explanation_simple: Motion capture (mocap) records real human movement and applies it to 3D characters. Actors wear special suits with markers (or use markerless AI systems), and the mocap system tracks the position of each marker to create realistic animation. This is how games like The Last of Us, Red Dead Redemption 2, and God of War get such realistic character movement. Retargeting is the process of taking mocap data from one character skeleton and applying it to a different character skeleton (like making a 7-foot troll move like a 6-foot actor).
key_concepts: Optical Mocap: Markers on suit tracked by multiple cameras (Vicon, OptiTrack)
Inertial Mocap: Sensors on body track movement via accelerometers (Xsens, Rokoko)
Markerless Mocap: Camera-only tracking using AI (Move.ai, DeepMotion)
Facial Mocap: Head-mounted camera tracks facial expressions (Faceware, LiveLink Face)
Finger Mocap: Gloves with sensors for hand/finger movement (Manus VR)
Mocap Cleanup: Fixing artifacts in raw mocap data (foot sliding, ground penetration, noise)
Retargeting: Mapping animation from one skeleton to another (different proportions, bone counts)
Root Motion: The character's root bone moves with animation (not just in-place animation)
Motion Builder: Industry standard for editing and cleaning mocap data (Autodesk)
IK Retargeting: Using IK to fix foot placement on uneven terrain
Motion Matching: System that selects the best animation clip based on character state (used in AAA)
Motion Warping: Adjusting animation timing to hit specific targets (syncing to gameplay events)
